newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK manufacturers seen struggling in Jan.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK manufacturers seen struggling in Jan.

text.p: British manufacturers are likely to have struggled in January, with no let-up from the strong pound and a further spate of destocking hampering output, economists said.
Production data for the month, due on Wednesday, are forecast to show manufacturing output rose by 0.3 percent in the month, slightly higher than December's 0.2 percent.
This would give a year-on-year rate of 1.5 percent, compared with December's 1.4 percent.

"Although export orders have been hit by sterling's strength, both the CBI and CIPS surveys suggest that domestic orders are rising and that output is on a steady, but modest, upward trend," said John O'Sullivan, UK economist at NatWest Markets.
But he said the surveys revealed that January was a month of destocking, so new orders were in part met from stocks.
The pound's steady upward climb -- it has gained around 16 percent on a trade-weighted basis since August -- has been a major headache for British firms, pushing up the price of their goods abroad.
But O'Sullivan said January producer prices data showed firms were restrained in new year pricing. "This will have helped their volumes."
The purchasing managers' or CIPS survey showed a strong rise in output during the month, leading some analysts to wonder if fears over the strong pound's effect on industry had been overdone.
But Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, said the impact of sterling's spirited rally is yet to be fully felt and makes it hard for manufacturers to be optimistic this year.
"It is important to remember that the forward looking Confederation of British Industry's monthly trends survey gives a far gloomier picture," Loynes said.

Its latest report showed export demand weakened in January and February. "The output balance has now lost all the ground it gained towards the end of last year and is perilously close to signalling falling manufacturing output over the next few months," Loynes said.
Overall industrial production, a wider measure which includes energy output and supply, has fared better than manufacturing over the winter months due to a surge in demand for oil and gas.

But the Reuters' consensus forecast suggests this may soon come to an end. It forecasts the rate of growth in production eased in January, up just 0.2 percent compared with December's 0.6 percent rise.
This would still allow the year-on-year rate of growth to pick up, to 2.7 percent from 1.9 percent in December.

"Industrial production was boosted ahead of manufacturing in December by the sharp rise in oil and gas output, but this will be partly reversed in January," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.
